results.summary: This project is a custom 8-bit RISC-V-inspired CPU with a hardware multiplier and 32B RAM. It uses a multi-cycle FSM for execution and supports a bootloader mode for program loading via specific input pins. The CPU outputs register values and the program counter for debugging. External hardware like a logic analyzer or LEDs is recommended for testing, along with a clock source.

DUMB-Turing is a Verilog implementation of a Turing machine based on Turing's original mathematical construction. It utilizes external SPI ROM and RAM for its transition table and tape, supporting 128 states and an alphabet size of 256. Testing this design is complex and requires pre-loading the SPI memory devices with data. The project requires one 512Kbit ROM and one 512Kbit RAM, which can be emulated by an on-board RP2040.

This design implements a custom SPI module to interface with RHD2164 neural amplifier chips and select specific channels for data transfer to a MCU via SPI. It also includes a register bank accessible by SPI or a scanchain/shift register. Testing instructions are not yet available, but it can be tested with an FPGA and emulators, or by connecting to actual RHD2164 chips and an MCU. External hardware includes the RHD2164 chip and an MCU.

This project aims to create graphics prototypes for a scaled-down Spacewar game, adhering to old demoscene specifications like VGA and audio. It utilizes SNES controller PMODs for input and outputs VGA signals. Testing with CocoTB is planned for the future. The design requires external VGA hardware and SNES PMODs.

Underflow Cubed is a four-tile demo for the TTSKY26a competition, featuring a custom per-scanline rendering algorithm derived from ray tracing. It includes a 24-voice synthesizer with delta-sigma modulation and supports multiple musical scales and keys. The design can be tested by connecting a TinyVGA and an audio Pmod, with inputs allowing for speedup adjustments. External hardware includes a TinyVGA and an audio Pmod.

This project displays a 12-hour clock by rendering three triangles using a race-the-beam triangle renderer, synchronized with VGA timing. The clock hands are updated each frame by indexing into tables for edge equations. It can be tested by connecting a TinyVGA to the output port and adjusting input pins to control the minute and hour hands. The TinyVGA is required external hardware for this design.

This project is a V2 systolic binary neural network accelerator designed for AI/ML tasks, featuring a 16-neuron XNOR dot product engine with hardware feature expansion and a balanced popcount tree. It uses an 8-cycle systolic compute to reuse hardware, reducing silicon footprint. No external hardware is required, but a Raspberry Pi or Arduino can load weights and run inference via the input pins. The design is documented in two versions, detailing its evolution.

Cgates tests two different implementations of Muller's C-gate, one using a latch and the other combinatorial logic, and evaluates their performance in four, sixteen, and sixty-four stage rings. The C-gate holds its previous state unless its two inputs are equal, at which point it takes on that value. Testing involves observing the output pins to verify C-gate behavior and ring oscillation frequencies, requiring an oscilloscope for detailed analysis. The design is intended to represent the best-case delay for an asynchronous pipestage.

This project is a placeholder with the description 'It works'. The available documentation is minimal, providing no details on its functionality, testing procedures, or required external hardware. The project utilizes several input and output pins, but their specific purpose is not defined. Due to the lack of information, the confidence in any specific tags or summary is low.

This design implements a 32-bit multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit for tiny ML accelerators, featuring a 7x8-bit multiplier that produces a 15-bit product per clock. A controller FSM manages partial sums and bias alignment across four training phases or a single inference phase. Testing is performed using Cocotb, comparing RTL against a reference Python script for various cycles and paths. No external hardware is required beyond the Tiny Tapeout carrier, with a host MCU able to stream weights and bias.
